_**Agent (gpt-5.6-sol 2026-07-30 11:05:23Z)**_

The short answer: DeadReckon has built much of the hard execution kernel, but it has not yet delivered the complete original experience.

Today it is a serious local verified-run system. It is not yet a dependable “start this goal, walk away, and trust it to keep working until the goal is genuinely complete” product.

## Where the project stands

| Original promise | Current state | Assessment |
|---|---|---|
| Define “done” before starting | Plain English can be compiled into `acceptance.yaml`; an LLM critic looks for weak checks and goals a stub could satisfy | Strong, although users can still fall back to detected project tests instead of consciously approving a real contract |
| Run coding CLIs in isolation | Git worktree and copy isolation are mature; changes require deliberate promotion | Strong for source isolation |
| Keep running until the goal is met | A normal run is foreground and limited to 12 turns; recovery normally requires `resume`. Chain has detached execution; current uncommitted plan work adds orphan adoption | Major remaining gap |
| Independently judge completion | A separate gate runs deterministic checks and validates the completion marker | Strong deterministic floor, but not the semantic meta-judge described in the original vision |
| Resist a dishonest worker | The worker cannot bypass a failing test merely by claiming completion; tamper checks catch several forms of weakening | Useful protection, but current “cannot forge” language overstates the boundary |
| Capture the whole run | State, snapshots, events, traces, spend, provenance, implementation notes and reports are persisted | One of the strongest parts of the system |
| Make the experience pleasant | The default five-command interface is quite good | Internally, too many execution models and advanced commands still leak into the mental model |

The most important correction is about the judge. The LLM currently helps write and critique the definition of done in [acceptance.rs](/Users/gdc/deadreckon/crates/deadreckon/src/commands/acceptance.rs:642). Final acceptance is then deterministic. There is no independent LLM reading the original goal, the resulting change and the evidence and deciding whether the goal was semantically achieved.

That means the original `/goal` idea is only partly present: semantic judgment happens before execution, not at the final boundary.

The current run loop also has a real ceiling: normal runs configure 12 turns in [run.rs](/Users/gdc/deadreckon/crates/deadreckon/src/commands/run.rs:496), after which the loop fails with a budget-exhausted state. State is durable, but the worker is not automatically durable. If its supervising process disappears, the job waits for an operator to resume or adopt it.

## What has genuinely been achieved

DeadReckon now has a credible “verified run” primitive:

1. Create an isolated workspace.
2. establish a completion contract;
3. run a chosen coding CLI;
4. retain state and evidence after every turn;
5. respond to gate failures with another corrective turn;
6. accept only after the external gate passes;
7. deliberately promote or export the result.

That is substantial. The current working tree passed the complete workspace test suite: 2,049 tests passed and none failed. I did not modify the repository.

The evidence system is also unusually thorough. [RunView](/Users/gdc/deadreckon/crates/deadreckon-core/src/run_view.rs:20) gives a useful read model over persisted state and ledgers. The promotion boundary in [promotion.rs](/Users/gdc/deadreckon/crates/deadreckon-core/src/promotion.rs:25) makes “completed” meaningfully different from “applied to my repository.”

So this is not a speculative pile of commands. It contains a real, tested kernel.

## Necessary complexity

These are inherent to the product and should remain:

- Safely isolating and later promoting source changes.
- Supporting different CLI providers and their different streaming, cancellation and accounting behaviour.
- Durable job identity, state, locking, recovery and cancellation.
- Compiling acceptance criteria into executable checks.
- A semantic judge for requirements that cannot be reduced to tests.
- Preventing the worker from modifying its own acceptance mechanism.
- Recording enough evidence to explain why a result was accepted.
- Scheduling dependent and parallel units of verified work.
- Explicit budgets, deadlines and blocked states. “Until done” must not mean “loop forever.”

## Incidental complexity

This is complexity created by the current shape of the implementation rather than the underlying problem:

- Forty-five top-level command variants, even though most are hidden from ordinary help.
- Several overlapping journey concepts: run, chain, plan/fork/merge, campaign, reshape and others.
- Control truth spread across state JSON, several JSONL ledgers and sidecar files, requiring hand-written reconciliation and orphan adoption.
- Repeated provider, retry, narration and budget policies in different orchestration layers.
- Multiple documentation and narration pipelines.
- Compatibility aliases, no-op flags and old spellings.
- Making implementation-note production part of the completion ritual, rather than deriving the after-state account from captured evidence.
- Continuing to deepen campaigns, learning, narration and other secondary systems before unattended goal execution is fully dependable.

The architectural smell is: there is one good verified-run atom, but too many ways to arrange and supervise it.

## The trust-boundary problem

The README’s “it can’t fake the finish” claim is stronger than the current implementation warrants.

The gate nonce is stored inside the run directory, and the marker uses Rust’s `DefaultHasher` in [gate.rs](/Users/gdc/deadreckon/crates/deadreckon-core/src/gate.rs:752), rather than a cryptographic MAC or signature. General CLI-provider and Bash-tool execution do not consistently deny access to gate material. In addition, automatic sandbox selection can fall back to no sandbox.

The system can truthfully say:

> A separate process runs the acceptance checks, and an existing completion marker cannot make failing checks pass.

It cannot yet universally say:

> A hostile coding agent is technically unable to forge acceptance.

Results should distinguish:

- `VERIFIED + CONFINED`
- `VERIFIED + UNCONFINED`
- `NEEDS REVIEW`
- `FAILED`

That would make the confidence claim precise rather than absolute.

## Where I would take it next

### 1. Finish the durable goal executor

Make `deadreckon start` create a durable local job, return its ID and detach by default. A small supervisor or user service should:

- lease pending jobs;
- recover abandoned leases;
- restart after terminal or machine failure;
- retain bounded retry, spend and time policies;
- distinguish blocked, cancelled, budget-exhausted and failed;
- supervise runs, chains and plans through the same scheduler.

Temporal is the useful exemplar here. Its core model is a durable execution reconstructed from an append-only event history, with explicit lifecycle operations such as start, describe, result, cancel, terminate and reset. DeadReckon should extract those durability and operator-semantics patterns without becoming a distributed workflow platform. [Temporal workflow execution](https://docs.temporal.io/workflow-execution), [Temporal CLI workflow commands](https://docs.temporal.io/cli/command-reference/workflow).

### 2. Restore the semantic meta-judge as a second key

Completion should require:

1. Deterministic checks pass.
2. An independent, read-only semantic judge assesses the goal, contract, diff and evidence.

The semantic judge must never override failed deterministic checks. It should return `achieved`, `revise` or `uncertain`, with evidence-backed reasons. If it is unavailable in strict mode, the result becomes `NEEDS REVIEW`, not accepted.

This is necessary complexity: natural-language goals cannot always be completely compiled into tests.

### 3. Close the gate boundary

- Keep signing material outside the agent-visible workspace.
- Use HMAC-SHA-256 or a proper signature.
- Deny gate and proof paths across every provider and tool route.
- Bind the receipt to the contract, policy, source revision and resulting revision.
- Fail closed for unattended trusted runs.
- Add adversarial tests in which an agent deliberately searches for and attempts to forge the marker.

### 4. Collapse the product around one job model

Keep the ordinary surface:

```text
start
attach
status
list
finish
```

Plans, chains and campaigns should become internal scheduling shapes or an explicitly advanced namespace. They should all create the same durable jobs and verified-run receipts.

Similarly, create one append-only control event history and derive current state and `RunView` from it. Rich spend, trace and documentation evidence can remain separate, but lifecycle truth should have one source.

### 5. Freeze secondary expansion and dogfood the promise

Temporarily freeze deeper campaign features, learning/improve surfaces and additional narration variants. Test the core promise on 20–30 real tasks across multiple repositories and providers.

Measure:

- unattended verified completion rate;
- automatic recovery rate;
- false acceptance and false rejection;
- number of operator interventions;
- time required to understand the final result;
- supervision and judging cost.

Kill the terminal, worker and machine during these trials. Remove network access. Attempt to tamper with the gate. Run DeadReckon on DeadReckon itself.

## Bottom line

DeadReckon contains a strong, unusually well-tested verified-run kernel inside an overgrown product.

The next phase should not be more orchestration features. It should make one promise completely true:

> Give DeadReckon a goal and an approved definition of done. It will work in isolation, survive interruptions, stop for explicit bounded reasons, independently verify both the checks and the meaning of the result, and leave behind a clear receipt explaining what happened.

Once that experience is reliable and pleasant, the plans, chains and campaigns become valuable multipliers instead of competing product models.

_**Agent (gpt-5.6-sol 2026-07-30 11:05:23Z)**_

_**Agent (gpt-5.6-sol 2026-07-30 11:05:23Z)**_

“Finish the durable goal executor” means making DeadReckon responsible for the job after the user starts it.

Right now, DeadReckon has durable records, but not fully durable execution.

## Today

A normal run behaves roughly like this:

```text
Your terminal
    ↓
deadreckon run
    ↓
coding CLI
    ↓
gate
```

The `deadreckon run` process is the supervisor. While that process is alive, it keeps giving the coding CLI turns and checking the result.

DeadReckon saves enough state to recover, but:

- closing the supervisor stops the work;
- restarting the computer stops the work;
- someone must run `resume`;
- a normal attempt stops after 12 turns;
- detached execution exists for chains, but is not the common execution model.

That is resumable execution: “we can pick up where we stopped.”

It is not yet durable execution: “DeadReckon continues to own the job until it reaches a legitimate stopping point.”

## The proposed experience

The user should be able to do this:

```bash
deadreckon start "Add password reset"
```

DeadReckon would:

1. Create the isolated workspace.
2. Prepare and approve the definition of done.
3. Record a durable job.
4. Return a run ID immediately.
5. Let a background supervisor carry on.

```text
Started run dr-4821
Workspace: isolated
Status: running
Attach: deadreckon attach dr-4821
```

The terminal is no longer responsible for keeping the work alive.

```text
Terminal                 DeadReckon supervisor
   │                              │
   ├── start goal ───────────────→│
   │←── run ID ───────────────────┤
   │                              ├── run coding CLI
   │                              ├── save evidence
   │                              ├── run gate
   │                              ├── retry if appropriate
   │                              └── finish or stop explicitly
   │
   └── may close safely
```

`attach` would only observe or interact with the job. Disconnecting would not stop it.

## What keeps it durable

The background supervisor needs four basic mechanisms.

### A durable queue

`start` writes the goal into a local queue before execution begins:

```text
Job: dr-4821
Goal: Add password reset
Contract: acceptance.yaml
State: queued
Budget: $20
Deadline: 4 hours
Workspace: /path/to/worktree
```

If no supervisor is currently running, DeadReckon starts one.

### Leases and heartbeats

When a supervisor takes a job, it records:

```text
dr-4821 is leased by process 9312 until 14:35:00
```

It renews that lease periodically.

If the process crashes, the lease expires. Another supervisor can safely adopt the job. This prevents both abandonment and two supervisors working the same job simultaneously.

The uncommitted plan changes currently in the repository are moving towards this kind of orphan adoption, but it should become a shared facility for every execution shape.

### Checkpoints after every important event

DeadReckon already persists much of this. The durable executor would formalize events such as:

```text
Job started
Turn 1 started
Turn 1 completed
Gate failed
Corrective turn requested
Turn 2 completed
Gate passed
Semantic judge passed
Run verified
```

After a crash, the replacement supervisor reads this history and knows what to do next. It does not start the entire job again.

### Explicit stopping reasons

“Keep running until done” should not mean infinite retries.

A job may stop because it is:

```text
VERIFIED
BLOCKED — requires user decision
BUDGET_EXHAUSTED
DEADLINE_REACHED
FAILED — unrecoverable error
CANCELLED
```

Those states are part of the confidence model. Quietly dying because a terminal closed is not.

## It does not require a large distributed system

This could initially be a small local service:

```text
deadreckond
```

On macOS it could run through `launchd`; Linux could use a user-level `systemd` service. DeadReckon could also begin with a simpler detached conductor process, provided it has leases and automatic adoption.

It does not need Kubernetes, a server database or a cloud account. SQLite or an append-only local event log would be sufficient.

## Why this is the highest-priority gap

The original promise is not primarily “we save excellent records.” It is:

> Give the system a goal and trust it to carry responsibility for reaching a verified conclusion.

Without a durable executor, the human still carries part of that responsibility:

- keeping the process alive;
- noticing that it stopped;
- deciding whether to resume;
- restarting orchestration after a crash.

With it, the human only intervenes when DeadReckon produces an intentional `BLOCKED` state.

A practical definition of done for this feature would include:

- Start a run and close the terminal: it continues.
- Kill the coding CLI: DeadReckon retries or records a clear failure.
- Kill the supervisor: another supervisor adopts the run.
- Restart the computer: unfinished jobs resume automatically.
- Never run the same turn twice concurrently.
- Respect spend, time and retry limits.
- Preserve the same run ID, workspace and evidence throughout.
- Finish only through the normal verification boundary.

That change would turn DeadReckon from a well-persisted foreground runner into the “start it and trust it” product described in the original goal.

_**Agent (gpt-5.6-sol 2026-07-30 11:05:23Z)**_

DeadReckon now has a credible first Watchkeeper implementation. It is substantially closer to the product promise, but the full claim still needs real-world dogfooding and reboot testing.

### What works now

- `start` creates a durable Job, returns its ID and detaches.
- An append-only event history is the lifecycle source of truth.
- Fenced leases support abandoned-work recovery without changing Job identity.
- Runs stop with explicit reasons: blocked, cancelled, budget exhausted, retries exhausted, failed or needs review.
- Single, Graph and Campaign guided starts use the shared Job supervisor.
- Completion requires both:
  1. native deterministic checks;
  2. a fresh, read-only semantic judge.
- Failed deterministic checks never reach the semantic judge.
- Unavailable or uncertain judging fails closed as `NEEDS_REVIEW`.
- HMAC-authenticated receipts bind the approved goal, contract, policy, source and result.
- Gate keys remain outside agent-visible workspaces.
- `status`, `attach`, `report` and `finish` understand Jobs.
- Applying a verified result records an idempotent delivery event.
- Supervisor service commands are available for machine-restart recovery.

A live Single-job trial demonstrated detached start, isolated execution, deterministic verification, semantic achievement, receipt validation and successful delivery. The complete `make verify` gate also passed.

### Self-assessment

The necessary complexity is now concentrated around:

- immutable approved authority;
- append-only lifecycle events;
- fenced leases and process supervision;
- bounded policies and explicit outcomes;
- isolation;
- deterministic plus semantic verification;
- authenticated receipts;
- crash-safe parent recovery.

The remaining incidental complexity is mostly the older overlapping machinery:

- legacy Run, Plan, Chain and Campaign state paths;
- direct commands that do not yet use the Job scheduler;
- multiple narration and learning surfaces;
- deep Campaign behavior;
- auto-continuation variants.

Those should be consolidated or frozen, not expanded.

### What remains before making the full promise

- Execute the 24-task dogfood matrix; every row is deliberately still marked `not_run`.
- Test actual machine reboot recovery with an installed supervisor service.
- Run live Graph and Campaign trials, not only fixture and recovery tests.
- Kill terminals, workers and networks during trials and attempt receipt forgery.
- Move direct `run`, `orchestrate`, `chain` and `campaign` paths onto Jobs.
- Design safe parent repair. Graph and Campaign semantic `revise` currently stop at `NEEDS_REVIEW`.
- Add aggregate Campaign time and resource accounting.
- Fix the minor post-delivery UX gap where status remains verified and may still recommend `finish`, although delivery is recorded in history.

So the honest current promise is:

> Give DeadReckon a goal and an approved definition of done. Guided Single, Graph and Campaign work can run as durable isolated Jobs, stop for bounded reasons, verify checks and meaning independently, and produce an authenticated receipt. Process recovery is implemented; full machine-restart and field reliability remain to be proven.

_**Agent (gpt-5.6-sol 2026-07-30 11:05:23Z)**_

We have moved from architecture into a working, integrated implementation. The core mechanism is largely built; the remaining gap is proving it under sustained real-world use.

### What now works

- `start` creates a durable local job, returns its ID, and detaches.
- Jobs retain their workspace, budget, attempt history and lifecycle across worker or supervisor interruption.
- Runs, plans, chains and campaigns now converge on the same durable scheduler.
- Terminal outcomes distinguish blocked, cancelled, failed, budget exhausted, retry exhausted and needs review.
- Deterministic checks must pass before completion.
- An independent semantic judge then assesses whether the result actually satisfies the goal.
- If semantic judgment is unavailable in strict mode, the job becomes `NEEDS_REVIEW`—never falsely accepted.
- Completion receipts use HMAC-SHA-256, bind the contract, policy and revisions, and detect later mutation.
- Signing material and proof paths are kept outside the agent-visible workspace.
- Provider errors are classified so fatal failures stop immediately while transient failures receive bounded retries.
- Result application/export is tracked separately from whether the work was verified.

The operator contract is documented in [WATCHKEEPER-OPERATOR-ACCEPTANCE.md](/Users/gdc/deadreckon/docs/WATCHKEEPER-OPERATOR-ACCEPTANCE.md).

### Evidence so far

- Full `make verify`: passed.
- Release build and strict clippy: passed without warnings.
- Credential-free adversarial trials: **7 passed, 0 failed**.
- Those trials cover terminal detachment, killed workers, supervisor restart, network denial, gate-key attacks, receipt mutation and result delivery.
- Existing suites include 179 orchestration tests, 125 Chain tests and extensive Job, gate, receipt, provider and fault-matrix coverage.

### What is not proven yet

The central promise is not yet fully validated in live operation:

- Only 2 of the planned 24 live-provider tasks have been attempted.
- Neither live attempt reached verified completion.
- We have not yet performed a real machine-reboot recovery.
- Live provider interruption and restoration still need testing.
- A genuine cross-provider hostile gate attack remains untested.
- We have not completed the planned 20–30-task dogfood programme.
- A human operator has not yet run the acceptance checklist end to end.

So my honest assessment is:

> The necessary machinery exists and is strongly tested. We have not yet earned confidence in the complete product promise through live dogfooding.

_**Agent (gpt-5.6-sol 2026-07-30 11:05:23Z)**_

Yes. Some of the time was justified, but too much of it came from scope expansion and integration friction.

The necessary reasons were:

- This was not one feature. It combined a durable scheduler, recovery leases, process supervision, unified orchestration, semantic judging, cryptographic receipts, sandbox hardening and adversarial testing.
- DeadReckon already had separate execution models for runs, plans, chains and campaigns. Unifying them meant preserving their different budgets, recovery rules, apply behavior and historical state.
- The trust boundary required fail-closed behavior. A superficial implementation could have falsely declared work verified, so gate keys, receipts, sandbox routes and promotion all needed adversarial coverage.
- The repository’s verification suite is large. Full Rust builds, clippy and hundreds of tests take meaningful time.

The incidental reasons were:

- We attempted too much convergence in one tranche: **114 files and roughly 25,700 added lines**.
- Existing compatibility behavior forced numerous exceptions, especially around historical chains, foreground execution and sandbox `none`.
- Documentation, tests and code described different generations of the architecture. I just found canonical docs still claiming direct commands were process-owned after the code had made them durable.
- Some test failures cascaded from one boundary, but diagnosing them initially looked like dozens of separate defects.
- There was also an unusually long tooling/approval wait during the most recent commit operation.

My candid assessment: the implementation is substantial, but we should have delivered it as smaller observable milestones:

1. Durable Single Job.
2. Semantic second key and receipt.
3. Crash recovery and user service.
4. Graph/plan convergence.
5. Chain and campaign convergence.
6. Dogfood and documentation.

That would not necessarily reduce total engineering effort, but it would have made progress easier to inspect and prevented a large “everything changes together” integration phase.

From here, I would stop adding architecture. The remaining work should be narrowly constrained to correcting current documentation, running the live trials, fixing only defects those trials reveal, and preparing the six local commits for review and integration.

The necessary complexity was durability, lease fencing, immutable authority, sandboxed gate signing, two independent completion keys and append-only evidence.

We have added lifecycle fences intended to prevent public legacy commands from mutating state owned by a durable Job:

That checkpoint uncovered important architectural gaps, which is why it has not been committed yet.

## Still on the docket

### 1. Finish trusted driver authentication

The audit found that the hidden `supervisor drive` route could establish trusted driver state using a forgeable environment variable containing the Job ID.

A private release-token mechanism has been started, but it still needs to be wired through:

- initial leaf execution;
- resumed leaf execution;
- Graph and campaign drivers;
- spoofing tests;
- restart and trust-boundary tests.

A Job ID must identify work; it must not authorize control of that work.

### 2. Fix nested Plan ownership

Top-level Plans now mostly retain one Job identity. Nested subplans do not yet reliably do so.

At present, a nested Plan can:

- fail to inherit the root Job’s mutation fence;
- create an accidental second root Job;
- be mutated through public merge or kill paths;
- lose the trusted driver context when it shells out to child commands.

Ownership needs to be resolved recursively from every subplan back to one root Job.

### 3. Replace subordinate environment checks with a capability

The current subordinate-child route checks persisted state and environment metadata, but those values are predictable. It does not yet prove that the caller is the exact child approved in the frozen schedule.

The capability should bind:

- Job and attempt;
- active lease epoch;
- task ID;
- launch directory;
- provider;
- goal and contract;
- budget;
- non-terminal Job state.

### 4. Complete Chain convergence

Legacy Chain execution is being closed, but several edges remain:

- refuse unsupported execution before invoking a potentially billable planner;
- stop status/help from recommending commands that will be refused;
- remove the publicly forgeable debug environment escape hatch;
- preserve harmless draft creation;
- route the supported shape through the same durable Job scheduler.

### 5. Verify and land the lifecycle checkpoint

Before committing it we still need:

- focused ownership and spoofing tests;
- nested-plan tests;
- restart-boundary tests;
- trust-boundary tests;

## Implemented and committed locally

Nine commits are currently on local `main`, ahead of `origin/main`.

### Durable Jobs

- A durable `Job`, event-history and lease protocol.
- Append-only lifecycle events as the source of operational truth.
- Detached execution supervised outside the initiating terminal.
- Renewable, fenced leases with stale-lease reclamation.
- Bounded retry, spend and time policies.
- Explicit terminal outcomes including verified, blocked, cancelled, failed and budget-exhausted.
- Recovery after supervisor and worker interruption.
- Crash-atomic worker launch: a worker cannot begin mutating state until its launch has been durably recorded.
- Single runs, Graph plans and Campaigns entering the durable scheduler.

### Independent verification

Completion now requires two keys:

1. Deterministic acceptance checks pass.
2. A fresh, read-only semantic judge assesses the goal, contract, result, diff and evidence.

The semantic judge can return achieved, revise or uncertain. It cannot override failed deterministic checks. A required judge being unavailable cannot silently produce success.

### Trusted receipts and gate protection

- HMAC-SHA-256 receipts.
- Signing material kept outside the agent workspace.
- Receipt binding to the goal contract, acceptance result, semantic judgment, source/result revisions and result-tree digest.
- Frozen authority and proof paths.
- Revalidation before promotion or `finish`.
- Synthetic or agent-authored completion evidence is rejected.
- Tampered or missing receipts fail closed.
- Tests exercise trust-boundary attacks and crash positions.

### Operator surface and documentation

The durable workflow is shaped around:

- `start`
- `attach`
- `status`
- `list`
- `finish`
- cancellation and supervisor recovery

There is also an extensive manual acceptance script covering detachment, lease recovery, worker death, semantic judging and receipt tampering: [WATCHKEEPER-OPERATOR-ACCEPTANCE.md](/Users/gdc/deadreckon/docs/WATCHKEEPER-OPERATOR-ACCEPTANCE.md).

### Dogfood infrastructure

- A 24-scenario trial matrix.
- Metrics for verified completion, intervention, recovery, judging, tampering and receipt validation.
- Credential-free adversarial scenarios.
- Tests ensuring the harness derives results from durable evidence rather than trusting its own narration.

The committed baseline passed `make verify`.

It currently adds:

- Explicit `owner_job_id` ownership for every Plan.

- Refusal of public `fork`, `merge` and hidden driver routes when a Plan belongs to a durable Job.
- Private authentication for the root Graph/Campaign driver.
- One-use delegated capabilities for:
  - Plan children
  - nested Plan forks
  - nested Plan merges
  - Campaign sub-plans
- Capabilities bound to the exact Job, lease, attempt, command arguments, working directory, scope and Plan definition.
- Tokens delivered through private stdin rather than predictable environment variables.
- Atomic consumption so a delegated invocation cannot be replayed.
- Cancelling a nested Plan routes to its root Job.

## Already implemented and committed

Nine commits are on local `main`, which is currently nine commits ahead of `origin/main`.

### Durable Job execution

- `deadreckon start` creates a durable Job and hands it to a detached supervisor.
- Jobs have append-only event histories, leases, heartbeats and recoverable projections.
- Abandoned work can be reclaimed after process failure.
- Child launch is crash-atomic: recovery can distinguish “prepared”, “released” and “actually running”.
- Retry, time and spend policies are persisted.
- Terminal outcomes distinguish verified, needs review, cancelled, failed and exhausted conditions.
- `start`, `attach`, `status`, `list` and `finish` operate around the Job abstraction.
- Run, Plan, Campaign and compatible Chain execution have been routed toward Jobs.

### Two-key completion

Completion now requires both:

1. Deterministic acceptance checks.
2. An independent semantic judgment.

The semantic judge returns achieved, revise or uncertain. Uncertain or unavailable strict judging becomes `NEEDS REVIEW`; it cannot override failed deterministic checks.

Synthetic or agent-authored completion evidence is rejected.

### Signed verification receipts

- Gate and receipt signing use HMAC-SHA-256.
- Signing material is stored outside the agent workspace.
- Receipts bind the approved authority, contract, launch plan, deterministic marker, semantic judgment, source revision, result revision and result tree.
- A modified result or judgment invalidates the receipt.
- `finish` accepts only a valid combined receipt.
- Provider and sandbox boundaries include protected-path controls and adversarial tests.

### Operator-facing documentation

The operator contract, architecture, concepts, schemas, acceptance checklist and `MAP-OF-DEADRECKON.md` were updated to describe this model.

### Initial dogfood machinery

There is now:

- a trial matrix;
- metrics collection;
- adversarial tampering scenarios;
- credential-free test results;
- crash and restart tests;
- tests for forged or synthetic completion evidence.

The committed baseline passed `make verify`.

## Implemented in the working tree, but not committed yet

This is the large hardening tranche produced after the subagent audits.

- Plans now record their owning Job.
- Nested Plans remain under one root Job instead of creating additional Jobs.
- Public `fork`, `merge`, repair and kill routes are fenced when a Job owns the Plan.
- Approved Plan definitions are frozen and checked across the complete parent/child lineage.
- Cycles, broken parent links and excessive nesting fail closed.
- Nested Plan recovery handles a crash after the child merged but before the parent recorded the result.
- Campaign schedules are frozen and cryptographically bound to delegated work.
- Delegated child capabilities bind the exact Job, action, arguments, directory, schedule and live lease.
- Capabilities are one-use and revoked on launch failure.
- Plaintext launch secrets were removed from persisted acknowledgements; descendants no longer inherit supervisor authentication variables.
- Delegation persistence received Unix directory syncing and non-UTF-8 argument support.
- Chain requests are being preflighted before paying a planner for a configuration that cannot execute.
- Chain status/help is being changed so it recommends durable migration or inspection instead of legacy `chain run` and `chain resume`.

## What the audits found still needs fixing

Four significant lifecycle gaps remain:

1. **Cancellation must always win.**  
   If cancellation arrives while an advanced child is running, its exit can currently enter recovery and relaunch work. It must finish exactly once as `Cancelled`, with no subsequent retry.

2. **Adopted advanced work needs normal recovery.**  
   A Graph or Campaign child adopted after supervisor loss is classified too early. It must follow the same bounded recovery rules as a normally launched child.

3. **Repair crashes between artifact creation and mapping.**  
   A crash after saving a root Plan/Campaign but before writing its Job mapping can strand valid work. Recovery must find that same artifact, validate its ownership, restore the mapping and preserve its real planner accounting—never create a replacement.

4. **Distinguish spend exhaustion from time exhaustion.**  
   Graph and Campaign failures need to retain a typed `SpendCap` or `WallCap` cause. Some current paths collapse these into `FatalProvider` or incorrectly report every budget failure as spend.

Work on the data structures for items 3 and 4 has begun, but it is mid-flight and not yet verified.

## What has been implemented

### 1. One durable Job model

`start` now creates a durable, detached Job with:

- a stable Job ID;
- append-only lifecycle history;
- leases and heartbeats;
- bounded retries;
- recovery after supervisor or worker interruption;
- explicit outcomes such as cancelled, blocked, budget exhausted, failed and needs review;
- `attach`, `status`, `list`, `report` and `finish` operations.

Direct runs, graphs/plans and campaigns now enter through this common supervisor instead of behaving as unrelated execution systems.

### 2. Two-key completion

A result cannot be accepted merely because an agent says it is done.

Completion requires:

1. Deterministic checks from the definition of done.
2. A separate, read-only semantic judge evaluating the goal, changes and evidence.

The semantic judge cannot overrule failed checks. Missing, malformed, synthetic or insufficient evidence fails closed instead of producing an accepted result.

### 3. Protected completion receipts

DeadReckon now creates authenticated receipts that bind the result to:

- the contract and policy;
- source and resulting revisions;
- deterministic evidence;
- semantic judgment;
- spend and timing information;
- delivery/promotion information.

Gate authority and signing material are kept outside the worker’s visible workspace. We added adversarial cases for forged acknowledgements, fabricated evidence and altered histories.

### 4. Crash-safe launching and recovery

Launching a coding CLI is now treated as a durable protocol:

- the launch is recorded before the worker is released;
- a private capability handshake controls release;
- PID, boot and process-start identity are recorded;
- an existing worker can be adopted after supervisor loss;
- stale or reused PIDs are rejected;
- crashes before release do not consume a logical attempt;
- cancellation wins over retry or later classification;
- terminal outcomes should be written only once.

Graph and Campaign recovery continue under the original Job and root artifact IDs rather than silently creating replacement work.

### 5. Durable nested work

The current hardening tranche adds:

- Campaign child Plan IDs reserved before launch;
- one-time delegation capabilities;
- frozen Plan/Campaign definitions and lineage;
- recovery from crashes between artifact creation and mapping publication;
- reconstruction of missing mappings without replanning;
- exact preservation of root planner usage;
- shared recovery rules for owned and adopted workers.

### 6. Bounded spend and time

Planner and worker accounting is being embedded in the durable artifacts rather than reconstructed from optional sidecars.

Spend-cap and wall-time exhaustion are now recorded as different typed reasons and propagated into the final Job outcome.

### 7. Documentation and dogfood infrastructure

We added:

- the durable operator contract;
- architecture and lifecycle documentation;
- an operator acceptance guide;
- a 24-task dogfood harness;
- seven passing credential-free adversarial scenarios;
- CI/release coverage for the special characterization executable.

## Why it has taken so long

The scope crossed every execution path in an established codebase. Crash safety is also unusually expensive: it is not enough to make the happy path work. Every write, process launch and state transition has to answer, “What happens if the machine dies immediately after this line?”

The necessary complexity is:

- durable history;
- leasing and fencing;
- stable identities;
- bounded recovery;
- two independent completion keys;
- budget enforcement;
- protected receipts.

The incidental complexity is mainly:

- migrating several older execution models without breaking them;
- parallel Plan, Chain and Campaign representations;
- compatibility and characterization-only pathways;
- filesystem durability differences across operating systems;
- repeatedly discovering obscure crash windows through adversarial tests.

So what is happening now is a hardening loop, not uncontrolled feature expansion. Tests expose a boundary, we make that boundary durable, and then test the adjacent boundaries. The remaining question is no longer “Can DeadReckon do this?” It is “Have we produced enough hostile evidence to trust that it consistently does this?”

## Features implemented

### Durable Job execution

DeadReckon now has a real durable Job layer above individual coding runs:

- immutable approved goal, definition of done and policy;
- append-only Job lifecycle;
- fenced leases so two supervisors cannot legitimately own one Job;
- detached supervision;
- process-group ownership and cancellation;
- recovery of abandoned attempts;
- bounded retries, spend and wall time;
- typed terminal outcomes such as completed, blocked, cancelled, failed and budget exhausted;
- persisted `JobView` state that `status`, `list`, `attach` and `finish` can read after the launching terminal disappears.

A user service can restart the supervisor after login. The machinery exists, but actual reboot recovery has not yet passed a live operator trial.

### Two independent completion decisions

A durable Job cannot complete merely because the coding agent says it is done.

The path now requires:

1. The deterministic definition-of-done gate passes inside the contained workspace.
2. A fresh, read-only semantic judge assesses the approved goal, contract, result, diff and evidence.
3. The supervisor validates both decisions before issuing the receipt and permitting promotion.

A failed deterministic gate cannot be overridden by the semantic judge. Semantic `revise` or uncertainty stops the Job without calling it verified.

### Protected gate and receipt boundary

The trust boundary was materially strengthened:

- native markers and final receipts use HMAC-SHA-256;
- signing material lives outside the delegated workspace;
- authority, gate, proof and receipt paths are protected from the coding agent;
- receipts bind the approved contract and policy to the source revision, resulting revision, evidence and confinement posture;
- uncontained or `sandbox none` execution cannot earn a strict verified receipt;
- `finish` revalidates the receipt before exporting or promoting the result;
- synthetic completion evidence and tampered receipts are rejected.

### Execution converging on one Job model

The following ordinary launches now create durable Jobs:

- direct `run` → Single Job;
- direct `orchestrate` → Graph Job;
- stored-plan `fork` → Graph Job;
- supported new chains → linear Graph Job;
- direct `campaign` → Campaign Job;
- guided `start` modes → the appropriate Job shape.

Graph and Campaign work produce a same-ID parent result. Child results are evidence; they do not independently declare the overall goal complete.

Some intentionally explicit compatibility paths remain outside this model: historical `chain run|resume`, chain extension, previews, and explicitly in-place or uncontained execution.

### Advanced Graph and Campaign recovery

The current uncommitted tranche adds substantial hardening:

- Plan and Campaign definitions are frozen and tied to the owning Job.
- Delegated child capabilities are scoped and single-use.
- Campaign sub-plan IDs are reserved before launch and recovered under the same identity.
- Missing `driver.json` mappings can be reconstructed without creating another root.
- Child launch is crash-atomic where durable linkage exists.
- Cancellation and terminal events are written only once.
- Boot-identity changes cannot accidentally adopt an unrelated reused PID.
- Chain shapes that cannot be translated honestly are refused instead of silently losing semantics.

### Aggregate budget enforcement

The latest work closes a serious hole found during the loop:

- root planner spend and wall time are preserved durably;
- planner use is subtracted before children receive budgets;
- remaining Plan budget is divided across tasks instead of giving every task the entire parent cap;
- Campaign children now receive wall limits as well as spend limits;
- recovery checks planner exhaustion before allowing child work to resume;
- Graph and Campaign planner exhaustion becomes a typed `SpendCap` or `WallCap`;
- crash-recovery tests assert that zero children launch once the root planner has consumed the approved budget.

Focused tests for these paths are passing. The full repository gate has not yet been rerun after the newest changes.

### Operator evidence

The implementation now leaves behind:

- Job events and projections;
- linked run evidence;
- spend and timing information;
- deterministic gate results;
- semantic judgment;
- source/result lineage;
- signed completion receipt;
- narratives and inspection/report surfaces.

The intended operator model is captured in the [architecture map](/Users/gdc/deadreckon/docs/MAP-OF-DEADRECKON.md:78) and the concrete [operator acceptance script](/Users/gdc/deadreckon/docs/WATCHKEEPER-OPERATOR-ACCEPTANCE.md:1).

## Bottom line

> Give DeadReckon a goal and an approved definition of done. It will work in isolation, survive interruptions, stop for explicit bounded reasons, independently verify both the checks and the meaning of the result, and leave behind a clear receipt explaining what happened.

We have implemented almost every noun and mechanism in that sentence. The unresolved phrase is “will survive interruptions” as an operator-trusted claim. Automated recovery and fault-injection coverage are substantial, but live terminal, service, reboot and cross-provider trials have not earned that confidence yet.

The next phase should therefore be verification, dogfooding and pruning—not another broad feature expansion.

## What we implemented

| Area | Current achievement |
|---|---|
| Durable job model | Added immutable job authority, append-only lifecycle events, fenced leases, attempt records, process ownership and recovery. |
| Detached execution | `start` creates a durable job, returns its ID and allows supervision to continue independently of the launching terminal. |
| Explicit stopping reasons | Jobs distinguish success, cancellation, blocking, failure, budget exhaustion and semantic uncertainty/revision. |
| Recovery | The supervisor can reclaim abandoned jobs, reject stale processes, recover incomplete launches and continue using the same parent ID. |
| Bounded execution | Attempt, wall-time and spend limits are persisted and enforced. Current hardening extends aggregate limits across plan tasks and campaign sub-plans. |
| Two-key completion | Deterministic checks must pass first. A fresh, read-only semantic judge must then return `achieved`. It can also return `revise` or `uncertain`. |
| Fail-closed judgment | A missing or invalid semantic judgment cannot produce an accepted result. It becomes `NEEDS_REVIEW`. |
| Tamper-resistant receipts | HMAC-SHA-256 receipts bind the approved authority, contract, revisions, evidence and result tree. `finish` revalidates them before promotion. |
| Gate boundary | Signing material and protected evidence paths are withheld from agent execution. Synthetic provider “success” evidence is rejected. |
| One scheduler | Ordinary runs become Single Jobs; orchestration, stored plans and supported chains become Graph Jobs; campaigns become Campaign Jobs. |
| Parent verification | Graph and Campaign results are verified and receipted as one parent result rather than trusting individual children. |
| Service support | Commands and definitions exist for managed launchd/systemd supervision. |
| Operator surfaces | Job-aware `start`, `attach`, `status`, `list`, reports and `finish` read durable state rather than depending on an active UI. |
| Dogfood infrastructure | Added a 24-row trial matrix, metrics collector, result schemas and credential-free adversarial tampering tests. |

The current uncommitted tranche further adds:

- exact ownership between a Job and its Plan or Campaign;
- crash-safe reservation and launch of campaign sub-plans;
- same-ID repair when intermediate mapping files disappear;
- aggregate planner and child budget accounting;
- recovery of persisted typed budget outcomes;
- cancellation winning cleanly during terminal classification;
- isolation of historical chain/orchestration characterization behind a separate feature-gated binary.

The complete verification gate passed, including formatting, Clippy with warnings denied, 790 main CLI tests, all workspace integration suites, feature-gated chain/orchestration suites and an optimized release build. The final independent audit found no blocking issue.

## What is still on the docket

### 1. Commit the current hardening tranche

It is ready for a carefully scoped local commit. It touches 29 tracked files plus one new ownership test. User-owned `.specstory`, editor and unrelated documentation changes must remain excluded.

### 2. Prove the promise using real work

This is now the largest gap. The dogfood kit currently records only two unsuccessful attempts, 22 unrun rows and zero live verified completions.

We still need to run 20–30 genuine tasks across:

- at least two repositories;
- multiple real provider routes;
- different task shapes and definitions of done;
- terminal, worker and supervisor termination;
- network loss and restoration;
- tampering attempts;
- a real login or machine reboot.

Then calculate intervention rates, recovery rates, false acceptance/rejection, time, spend and judging cost. The existing checklist describes this in [WATCHKEEPER-OPERATOR-ACCEPTANCE.md](/Users/gdc/deadreckon/docs/WATCHKEEPER-OPERATOR-ACCEPTANCE.md:380).

### 3. Add safe semantic repair for Graph and Campaign jobs

A Single Job can respond to semantic `revise` and try bounded corrective work. Graph and Campaign parents currently stop at `NEEDS_REVIEW`. They need a controlled repair path that preserves the original authority and receipt boundary.

### 4. Validate the user service for real

The launchd/systemd definitions and commands are implemented and hermetically tested. We have not yet demonstrated an installed service reclaiming work after an actual logout, login or reboot.

### 5. Finish provider and containment parity

Strict paths fail closed, but provider adapters do not all offer equivalent structured events, spend accounting or sandbox behavior. Subscription quotas and universal usage accounting remain incomplete.

### 6. Retire compatibility complexity

Historical `chain run|resume`, preview modes, unsupported conductor policies and some legacy run-oriented projections remain. Once the durable paths survive dogfooding, these should either be translated honestly onto Jobs or explicitly retired.

## The honest assessment

We have built most of the necessary machinery behind the desired statement:

> Give DeadReckon a goal and an approved definition of done. It will work in isolation, survive interruptions, stop for explicit bounded reasons, independently verify both the checks and the meaning of the result, and leave behind a clear receipt explaining what happened.

The code now supports that claim structurally and under extensive automated fault tests. We cannot yet make it as a fully demonstrated product claim because the live cross-provider, active-service, reboot and 20–30-task trials have not happened.

The correct next move is therefore to commit the completed hardening, freeze further feature expansion, and spend the next phase trying to break DeadReckon on real work. The current architectural status is also summarized in [MAP-OF-DEADRECKON.md](/Users/gdc/deadreckon/docs/MAP-OF-DEADRECKON.md:84).

## What we implemented

| Area | Current achievement |
|---|---|
| Durable Job model | Added immutable authority, Job identity, append-only lifecycle events, leases, retry policy, deadlines, budgets, semantic judgments and completion receipts. |
| Detached execution | `start` creates the Job before execution, returns its ID and lets a supervisor continue independently of the launching terminal. |
| Recovery | Added lease reclaim, process-group supervision, crash-atomic child launch, same-ID recovery and reconstruction of persisted Graph/Campaign work. |
| Typed stopping | Jobs distinguish `verified`, `needs_review`, `blocked`, `budget_exhausted`, `deadline_reached`, `retry_exhausted`, `cancelled` and `failed`, with specific causal stop reasons. |
| One Job scheduler | Ordinary single runs, orchestration/plans, new supported chains, stored-plan forks and campaigns now execute beneath a durable parent Job. |
| Deterministic verification | Approved definitions of done run inside a resolved sandbox. A failed deterministic check can never be overruled by an LLM. |
| Semantic second key | After checks pass, a fresh read-only judge assesses the goal, contract, diff and evidence as `achieved`, `revise` or `uncertain`. Unavailable or malformed judging fails closed as `NEEDS_REVIEW`. |
| Signed receipts | Completion receipts use HMAC-SHA-256 and bind the authority, approved contract, policy, launch plan, source/result revisions, deterministic proof, semantic judgment, containment and result-tree digest. |
| Gate isolation | Signing keys live outside the agent workspace. Gate, proof, Job and authority paths are denied or read-only across supported sandbox/provider routes. |
| Deliberate promotion | `finish` revalidates the complete receipt and current result before applying it to the source repository. |
| Operator surface | Jobs are resolved through `start`, `attach`, `status`, `list` and `finish`; reports and views derive from durable state. |
| Dogfood infrastructure | Added a 24-row operator kit, adversarial runner, metrics collector, schemas and the [operator acceptance checklist](/Users/gdc/deadreckon/docs/WATCHKEEPER-OPERATOR-ACCEPTANCE.md:1). |

This work is represented by ten local commits, from `79bb2e8` through `dce5e06`: approximately 36,000 inserted lines across 129 tracked files.

## What we have actually proven

We have now completed one real Codex-backed journey:

1. An approved definition of done initially failed.
2. `start` returned one detached Job ID.
3. Codex changed the isolated worktree.
4. The deterministic Cargo checks passed.
5. An independent read-only Codex judgment returned `achieved` with evidence-backed goal coverage.
6. DeadReckon created a valid, contained, two-key HMAC receipt.
7. Changing the receipt signature caused `finish` to refuse promotion.
8. Restoring the original receipt allowed `finish` to apply the result.
9. The resulting repository test passed and produced the requested output.

That is the first live demonstration of the intended sentence:

> Give DeadReckon a goal and an approved definition of done. It works in isolation, independently verifies both the checks and the meaning, and leaves a receipt explaining what happened.

The credential-free adversarial runner also recorded 7 passes, 0 failures and 5 explicitly unproven scenarios.

## Implemented, but not sufficiently proven yet

- Graph and Campaign Jobs can recover persisted ownership, budgets and mappings, but have not completed the full live interruption matrix.
- Supervisor service definitions exist for launchd and systemd, but machine-reboot recovery has not been demonstrated.
- Single Jobs can act on semantic `revise`; Graph and Campaign parents currently stop for review because safe parent repair is not implemented.
- Gate forgery, receipt mutation and protected-path attacks have strong automated coverage, but hostile cross-provider trials remain.
- Provider routes share the outer contract, but structured events, usage reporting and steering are uneven.
- Subscription-backed provider usage is not truly bounded by a dollar cap. One tiny live task reported more than 200,000 input tokens while recording $0.
- Narration and documentation work currently adds substantial latency and noise.

## Immediate defects found by dogfooding

These should be fixed before calling the tranche merge-ready.

1. The Codex semantic-judge adapter

The first live job failed closed because Codex JSONL transport events were passed to the semantic parser instead of the final structured answer. A four-file adapter fix is implemented, tested and was used successfully in the second live job, but it remains uncommitted.

2. Cleanup reports success when it failed

`finish --cleanup` applied the verified result, but a dirty worktree prevented removal. DeadReckon discarded both Git errors, claimed cleanup was complete and left the worktree and branch behind.

The fix must report “applied; cleanup incomplete,” preserve the successful delivery, verify removal postconditions, and support cleanup of a Job’s same-ID backing Run. It must not silently force-delete untracked evidence. The cause is in [lifecycle.rs](/Users/gdc/deadreckon/crates/deadreckon/src/commands/lifecycle.rs:1225).

3. Provider-private files leaked into the delivered result

SpecStory created `.specstory/**` files inside the writable worktree. DeadReckon treated every filesystem change as deliverable, staged with `git add -A`, signed those files into the result digest and promoted them.

We need one shared artifact policy used by:

- turn staging;
- semantic evidence;
- receipt hashing;
- finish preview and application.

Provider telemetry such as `.specstory/**` should remain private run evidence unless the approved contract explicitly allows it. ## What we have implemented

### 1. Durable detached Jobs

`deadreckon start` can now create a durable Job, return its ID, and run it detached.

The implementation includes:

- append-only Job lifecycle events;
- fenced leases and heartbeats;
- abandoned-lease recovery;
- supervisor restart and worker adoption;
- bounded attempts, spend and wall time;
- explicit terminal outcomes including completed, blocked, cancelled, failed, budget-exhausted and needs-review;
- PID and process-start identity to avoid adopting the wrong process;
- crash-atomic worker launching, so a crash between “starting” and “running” does not silently duplicate work;
- service-oriented supervision;
- same-ID ownership between the Job and its underlying run or plan.

This is the largest completed part of the work.

### 2. Runs, chains, plans and campaigns on the Job scheduler

Ordinary direct runs, supported chains, graphs, nested plans and campaigns now enter through the durable Job scheduler.

We also added:

- recovery of partially created parent/child relationships;
- recovery of reserved but not fully launched child work;
- aggregate parent and child spend/time limits;
- cancellation precedence during recovery;
- parent verification and receipt handling.

This is functional convergence. It is not yet a total removal of the older Run, Chain and Plan representations. Those remain for compatibility and internal execution.

### 3. Two-key completion

A successful Job now requires both:

1. Deterministic definition-of-done checks.
2. An independent, read-only semantic judgment.

The semantic judge receives the goal, approved contract, result diff and evidence. It returns an evidence-backed result such as achieved, revise or uncertain.

Important constraints are in place:

- semantic judgment cannot override a failed deterministic check;
- malformed or unsupported evidence is rejected;
- judging is budget-aware;
- synthetic completion evidence is rejected;
- unavailable semantic judging produces `needs_review`, rather than silently accepting the result.

A real Codex dogfood run initially exposed an adapter bug: Codex’s JSONL event stream was being parsed instead of its structured final judgment. That has been fixed and committed.

### 4. Protected receipts and gate authority

We now have HMAC-authenticated completion receipts that bind the result to its authority and verification evidence.

Implemented protections include:

- signing material outside the agent-visible workspace;
- protected gate paths;
- HMAC receipt authentication;
- source-authority binding;
- contract and policy binding;
- result revision and tree identity;
- deterministic and semantic evidence;
- refusal of corrupted, malformed, forged or over-budget evidence;
- validation before promotion or delivery.

In the real Codex run, the valid receipt was accepted, an altered signature was refused, and restoring the valid receipt allowed `finish` to apply the result.

### 5. Operator lifecycle

The ordinary surface now centres on:

```text
start
attach
status
list
finish
```

Jobs can be inspected through the same identity, and verified results can be promoted and delivered.

A live run exposed another bug: applying the result succeeded, but dirty-worktree cleanup failed while DeadReckon reported that it succeeded. That is now fixed:

- cleanup errors are no longer discarded;
- actual worktree and branch postconditions are checked;
- delivery remains recorded if apply succeeded;
- the outcome says “applied, cleanup incomplete”;
- explicit same-ID Job cleanup can recover the retained run;
- forceful deletion still requires explicit operator authority.

### 6. Documentation and adversarial infrastructure

We added:

- the durable execution goal and protocol;
- the operator contract;
- acceptance instructions;
- a 24-task, multi-repository/provider dogfood matrix;
- metrics collection;
- credential-free crash, evidence and tamper trials;
- recovery-boundary tests.

The credential-free adversarial suite currently records:

- 7 passed;
- 0 failed;
- 5 explicitly unproven.

Those unproven claims require real host or provider conditions and have not been converted into pretend test successes.

## What is currently being built

The live Codex run uncovered a third issue: provider-private `.specstory` files entered the result worktree and therefore affected parts of the signed and delivered result.

The uncommitted tranche introduces one central artifact classification:

- deliverable;
- evidence-only;
- lifecycle metadata;
- runtime-only.

The intended rule is:

- provider-private artifacts such as `.specstory/**` may remain in raw provenance;
- they must not count as product progress;
- they must not enter semantic diffs;
- they must not be committed to the result;
- they must not affect the deliverable receipt;
- they must not enter promoted libraries, parent plans or campaigns;
- `finish` must refuse a legacy result containing those files.

This work currently touches 14 source files and is not yet committed or fully verified.

## What we have implemented

### Durable Jobs

DeadReckon can now:

- create a durable Job before starting provider work
- return one Job ID and detach
- preserve an append-only lifecycle history
- lease work to a local supervisor
- heartbeat and reclaim expired leases
- adopt an existing child rather than automatically starting another
- keep attempt, spend, wall-time and deadline limits
- report typed outcomes such as verified, blocked, cancelled, budget exhausted, needs review and failed
- supervise Single, Graph and Campaign work through the Job layer
- generate launchd and systemd user-service definitions

We also fixed crash-sensitive areas such as child creation and advanced Graph and Campaign recovery.

### The ordinary command journey

The main operator journey now centres on:

```text
start → status/attach → finish
       list
```

These commands use the same Job identity and `JobView`.

Ordinary runs, orchestration, supported chains, stored-plan forks and campaigns now have Job-backed routes. Some older commands remain compatibility paths, including historical chain resume and explicit uncontained or in-place execution.

### Two-key completion

Strict completion now requires:

1. deterministic definition-of-done checks to pass
2. an independent semantic judge to assess the goal, contract, diff and evidence

The semantic judge returns `achieved`, `revise` or `uncertain`.

A failed deterministic check cannot be overridden. An unavailable or uncertain strict judge stops for review.

We also fixed the Codex adapter so structured semantic answers survive JSONL parsing.

### Signed completion receipts

DeadReckon now creates an HMAC-SHA-256 receipt using signing material outside the agent workspace.

The receipt binds the result to:

- the approved goal and contract
- the effective policy
- the source and result revisions
- deterministic evidence
- the semantic judgment
- containment information
- the stop reason
- the Job and run identities

`finish` validates the receipt before recording delivery. Tampered receipts are refused.

### More truthful lifecycle handling

We fixed several cases where DeadReckon previously reported more certainty than it had:

- incomplete workspace cleanup no longer reports success
- synthetic completion evidence is rejected
- stale or inconsistent authority information fails closed in more places
- finished results are compared with the Git objects actually delivered
- private paths appearing anywhere in result history are rejected, even if later deleted

### Artifact isolation

The current uncommitted tranche adds a shared distinction between:

- deliverable code and documentation
- provider evidence
- trusted lifecycle metadata
- runtime-only files

This is being applied across:

- provider turns
- semantic diffs
- receipt indexes
- promotion
- Graph and Campaign composition
- plans
- inspection
- learning
- source-authority checks
- `finish`

Provider-created `.specstory`, `.deadreckon`, `target` and `node_modules` content is now filtered from deliverable results. Raw provider evidence remains available in provenance archives.

The turn loop also rewrites provider-created Git history onto the approved base, restores trusted lifecycle metadata and reattaches a detached branch.

### Dogfood and acceptance tooling

We now have:

- a 24-task multi-repository, multi-provider matrix
- a metrics collector
- a credential-free adversarial runner
- a detailed operator acceptance checklist
- tamper, supervisor-kill, worker-kill, restart and network-loss procedures

- 0 failed
- 5 unproven

Read-only audit complete. The current code is substantially stronger, but the provider result boundary is not yet end-to-end closed.

## Correctness matrix

| Case | Sanitizer | Receipt | Finish/apply |
|---|---|---|---|
| Merge commits | Incomplete | Correct and merge-aware | Final tree only; not full delivery history |
| Non-UTF-8 paths | Lossy/incomplete | Correct on Unix; fails closed elsewhere | Refuses valid Unix paths |
| Symlinks | Correct on Unix | Binds raw target and kind on Unix | Git entry comparison is exact for UTF-8 paths |
| Executable mode | Correct on Unix | Correct on Unix | Git entry includes mode |
| Gitlinks/submodules | Incorrect | Incorrect | Git entry comparison itself is exact |
| Filters | Git applies configured filters | Works only while filter config/output stays stable | Git object identity is exact |
| Linked-worktree `.git` redirect | Correct for the main contained turn | Not independently routed through the trusted context | A later docs provider bypasses the boundary |

## Critical: a writable provider runs after the sanitizer

The main turn does the right sequence initially:

- Capture trusted lifecycle and Git control before the provider at [turn_loop.rs:249](/Users/gdc/deadreckon/crates/deadreckon-runtime/src/turn_loop.rs:249).
- Restore trusted `.git`, discard provider-created commits, stage only deliverables and create a DeadReckon-owned commit at [turn_loop.rs:3093](/Users/gdc/deadreckon/crates/deadreckon-runtime/src/turn_loop.rs:3093).
- Disable hooks and supply a fixed identity for that commit at [turn_loop.rs:3136](/Users/gdc/deadreckon/crates/deadreckon-runtime/src/turn_loop.rs:3136).

But that is not the last writable provider boundary. Afterward, both completion paths call `complete_run_docs` at [turn_loop.rs:667](/Users/gdc/deadreckon/crates/deadreckon-runtime/src/turn_loop.rs:667) and [turn_loop.rs:1066](/Users/gdc/deadreckon/crates/deadreckon-runtime/src/turn_loop.rs:1066).

CLI documentation providers are then launched with:

- `SandboxBackend::None`
- `WorkspaceAccess::ReadWrite`

at [polish.rs:214](/Users/gdc/deadreckon/crates/deadreckon-runtime/src/polish.rs:214) and [polish.rs:503](/Users/gdc/deadreckon/crates/deadreckon-runtime/src/polish.rs:503).

After that provider returns, `publish_docs_for_promotion` invokes `commit_docs_if_worktree`, which:

- trusts workspace `.deadreckon/codebase.json`;
- trusts the live `.git`;
- writes shared Git configuration;
- stages `docs` without first clearing other staged changes;
- runs repository hooks.

That path is at [docs.rs:401](/Users/gdc/deadreckon/crates/deadreckon-core/src/docs.rs:401) and [docs.rs:2188](/Users/gdc/deadreckon/crates/deadreckon-core/src/docs.rs:2188).

Therefore a documentation CLI can redirect `.git`, alter trusted run evidence, stage arbitrary source changes, or commit deliverable changes after the trusted sanitizer. The gate and judge run afterward, but neither proves that only the intended documentation output crossed this boundary.

Minimal fix:

1. Run documentation CLI providers in the configured enforceable sandbox with read-only workspace access. If none is available, skip LLM polishing or return `NEEDS_REVIEW`.
2. Let only DeadReckon write the parsed documentation response.
3. Commit documentation through the same trusted Git-control path, with hooks disabled and an explicitly empty index before staging only approved documentation paths.
4. Compare workspace and Git-control identities around the documentation subcall.
5. Add a hostile documentation-provider test that tries to rewrite `.git`, the trusted record, source files and the index.

## Merge history: receipt good, turn sanitizer incomplete

The receipt implementation is sound here. It:

- verifies the approved base is an ancestor;
- enumerates every revision in `base..result`;
- runs `diff-tree -m` for every commit;
- parses NUL-delimited paths.

See [completion.rs:445](/Users/gdc/deadreckon/crates/deadreckon-core/src/completion.rs:445). This catches side-branch commits and paths introduced only by merge conflict resolution.

The turn sanitizer uses a different implementation at [turn_loop.rs:3373](/Users/gdc/deadreckon/crates/deadreckon-runtime/src/turn_loop.rs:3373): `git log --name-only -z` without `-m`. I confirmed with a disposable merge that a `.deadreckon/forged.json` path introduced only in the merge tree was omitted by this command, while the receipt’s `diff-tree -m` found it.

Minimal fix: make the trusted sanitizer use the same revision-by-revision `rev-list` plus `diff-tree -m` algorithm, but routed through `TrustedGitControl`.

Test: construct two clean parents and a merge whose resolution alone introduces a non-deliverable path. Assert both sanitizer and receipt reject it. The existing merged-history test only exercises add/delete commits on a side branch.

## Non-UTF-8 paths: partial support only

Receipt inventories preserve raw Unix path bytes at [completion.rs:665](/Users/gdc/deadreckon/crates/deadreckon-core/src/completion.rs:665). The artifact hash also binds raw platform path identity at [flight.rs:628](/Users/gdc/deadreckon/crates/deadreckon-core/src/flight.rs:628). Those parts are correct.

The turn sanitizer converts NUL-delimited paths with `String::from_utf8_lossy` at [turn_loop.rs:3396](/Users/gdc/deadreckon/crates/deadreckon-runtime/src/turn_loop.rs:3396). It can therefore collapse distinct names and cannot pass the exact path back to Git.

Apply also converts every changed path with `Path::to_str` at [lifecycle.rs:773](/Users/gdc/deadreckon/crates/deadreckon/src/commands/lifecycle.rs:773), so a receipt that seals correctly on Unix cannot be finished if it changes a non-UTF-8 path.

Trusted worktree routing similarly rejects non-UTF-8 `gitdir` and `commondir` records at [turn_loop.rs:2811](/Users/gdc/deadreckon/crates/deadreckon-runtime/src/turn_loop.rs:2811) and [turn_loop.rs:2870](/Users/gdc/deadreckon/crates/deadreckon-runtime/src/turn_loop.rs:2870).

Minimal fixes:

- Parse sanitizer output into `PathBuf`, preserving Unix bytes.
- Always run `reset --mixed <trusted-head>` before trusted staging, removing the need for lossy path-specific index resets.
- Add an OS-string Git command helper and use `GIT_LITERAL_PATHSPECS=1` for `git_tree_entry`.
- Either support raw Unix `gitdir` records or document this as an explicit unsupported-workspace stop reason.

Tests should cover an invalid-UTF-8 deliverable through sanitizer, receipt and finish, plus an invalid-UTF-8 path under `.deadreckon`.

## Gitlinks/submodules are currently misrepresented

The filesystem model explicitly says Git-facing completion must validate `160000` gitlinks at [flight.rs:215](/Users/gdc/deadreckon/crates/deadreckon-core/src/flight.rs:215). That validation does not exist.

Receipt comparison materializes the result with `checkout-index` at [completion.rs:577](/Users/gdc/deadreckon/crates/deadreckon-core/src/completion.rs:577). `ArtifactFileIndex` ignores directories at [flight.rs:477](/Users/gdc/deadreckon/crates/deadreckon-core/src/flight.rs:477).

I confirmed that `checkout-index` materializes a `160000` entry as an empty directory. Consequently:

- an uninitialized submodule is absent from both indexes and is accepted without being bound into `result_tree_sha256`;
- an initialized submodule is traversed as ordinary files and normally rejected because the comparison side is empty;
- a provider can create an empty nested Git repository and cause DeadReckon’s broad `git add` to stage a gitlink.

Minimal safe fix for this tranche: reject deliverable `160000` entries with an explicit unsupported-result reason, both immediately after trusted staging and during receipt validation.

Full support requires a Git-tree artifact kind containing the gitlink commit OID, plus rules proving an initialized submodule’s HEAD and checked-out tree. Filesystem recursion alone cannot validate it.

Tests:

- empty/uninitialized gitlink;
- initialized submodule;
- hostile nested repository created by a provider;
- changed submodule OID relative to the approved base.

## Filters are conditionally correct, not durable

`checkout-index` applies configured smudge filters. I verified a blob containing `UPPER` was materialized as `upper` by the active filter. Thus the current comparison checks the working representation, not raw blob bytes.

That works while the filter is deterministic and its configuration remains unchanged. It has two problems:

- changing repository or global filter configuration after sealing can invalidate an otherwise unchanged receipt;
- a provider-controlled `.gitattributes` can select an operator-configured external filter, causing the privileged sanitizer or receipt verifier to execute that command.

The current receipt therefore depends on mutable, executable Git configuration that is not bound into the receipt.

Minimal policy: reject active external filters on strict deliverable paths before any `git diff`, `git add` or `checkout-index` operation. A richer design would snapshot and bind filter configuration and run conversion in containment.

Tests:

- deterministic filter initially succeeds;
- changing its smudge command after sealing does not silently redefine the artifact;
- a filter command cannot create a sentinel outside its verification scratch area.

## Symlinks and executable modes

On Unix, these are implemented correctly:

- symlinks are not followed;
- their raw targets and filesystem kind are hashed;
- executable and regular files are distinct;
- copying preserves symlinks and executable permissions.

See [flight.rs:419](/Users/gdc/deadreckon/crates/deadreckon-core/src/flight.rs:419) and [artifacts.rs:302](/Users/gdc/deadreckon/crates/deadreckon-core/src/artifacts.rs:302). The executable mismatch test with `core.filemode=false` is valuable evidence.

Limitations remain:

- Windows collapses executable files to regular files in the filesystem index.
- Windows cannot copy a dangling symlink because it follows the source to determine link type.
- With `core.symlinks=false`, the receipt describes the platform’s regular-file materialization while the signed Git revision still contains a symlink.

These are fail-closed or platform-materialization limitations, not the same acceptance hole as gitlinks, but should be explicit in the operator contract.

## Linked-worktree `.git` handling

Within the main contained turn, this is strong:

- sandbox construction protects the workspace `.git`, resolved worktree Git directory and common Git directory at [policy.rs:57](/Users/gdc/deadreckon/crates/deadreckon-sandbox/src/policy.rs:57) and [commands.rs:54](/Users/gdc/deadreckon/crates/deadreckon-sandbox/src/commands.rs:54);
- the pre-provider bytes are captured outside the workspace;
- regular-file redirection is archived and restored;
- every sanitizer Git command receives explicit trusted `--git-dir` and `--work-tree` arguments at [turn_loop.rs:3408](/Users/gdc/deadreckon/crates/deadreckon-runtime/src/turn_loop.rs:3408).

A `.git` symlink or directory replacement is archived and then deliberately refused rather than recovered at [turn_loop.rs:2996](/Users/gdc/deadreckon/crates/deadreckon-runtime/src/turn_loop.rs:2996). That is safe, but it means automatic recovery stops permanently until an operator repairs the leaf. This should be an explicit bounded stop reason if retained.

End-to-end, the documentation bypass above defeats this protection. Receipt and docs code also still use generic Git routing rather than the trusted context. The durable direction is to move `TrustedGitControl` into core and require every privileged Git operation—sanitizer, docs, receipt, promotion and finish—to use it.

## Delivery history has one remaining gap

Apply verifies exact signed Git tree entries, including mode and OID, at [lifecycle.rs:697](/Users/gdc/deadreckon/crates/deadreckon/src/commands/lifecycle.rs:697). It also rejects unexpected paths in the final `delivery_before..delivered` tree delta.

It does not inspect every commit introduced during delivery. A hook can add an unexpected path in one commit and delete it in a later commit; the final delta is clean, but the unwanted blob remains in operator history.

Use the same merge-aware history inventory over `delivery_before..delivered`, compare all touched paths against the signed path set, and add an add-then-delete hook test. Verification should also be transactional or roll back to `delivery_before` on failure; currently a failed post-apply identity check can leave the rejected commits in the target repository.

The highest-priority order is:

1. Close the post-sanitizer documentation-provider boundary.
2. Reject or correctly model gitlinks.
3. Unify the sanitizer with the receipt’s merge-aware, byte-safe history scanner.
4. Decide and enforce strict filter semantics.
5. Make finish byte-safe and history-complete.
